# Abstract

The territory of East Timor (Timor-Leste), occupying the eastern half of the Timor island orogen alongside the coastal exclave of Oecusse Ambeno and the oceanic islands of Atauro and Jaco (16.917 km² across 233 terrestrial cells), experienced one of the most violent and demographically turbulent transitions in twentieth-century decolonisation. Following four centuries of Portuguese maritime hegemony and administrative neglect, the Carnation Revolution of 1974 precipitated a swift withdrawal of colonial authority, culminating in brief factional civil conflict and a unilateral declaration of independence on 28 November 1975. Nine days later, on 7 December 1975, Indonesian armed forces launched a full-scale airborne and amphibious invasion, initiating twenty-four years of military occupation characterised by intense armed conflict, forced population displacement, encirclement campaigns and severe famine.

Reconstructed across three administrative divisions under MANDALA, the aggregate population declined sharply from 660k in 1975 to 555k in 1980, representing an absolute loss of 105.000 persons (-15,9% net demographic contraction; regional density receding from 39,01 to 32,81 persons per km²). The primary driver of this demographic collapse was military operations between 1977 and 1979, which drove hundreds of thousands of civilians into mountain redoubts before herding them into strategic relocation camps where starvation and epidemic disease caused catastrophic mortality. Following pacification and the stabilisation of food supplies during the 1980s, the population rebounded through high marital fertility and natural increase, climbing to 748k in 1990 and 850k on the eve of the historic 1999 referendum.

The popular consultation of August 1999 resulted in an overwhelming 78,5% vote for independence, provoking a scorched-earth campaign by departing security forces and pro-Indonesian militias that laid waste to over 70% of physical infrastructure and forcibly deported more than 250k residents across the western border into Indonesian West Timor. Following international intervention by INTERFET and administration by the United Nations Transitional Administration in East Timor (UNTAET), sovereign statehood was formally restored on 20 May 2002. An extraordinary post-independence baby boom elevated the total fertility rate above 7 children per woman in the early 2000s, driving national population to 923k in 2004, 1,07M in 2010, 1,18M in 2015, 1,34M in 2022 and 1,4M by 2025 (yielding an aggregate density of 83,05 persons per km²).

Throughout this fifty-year sequence, demographic distribution shifted decisively toward the Dili metropolitan basin. In 1975, Dili Metropolitan and the Central North Coast accommodated 250,8k residents (38% of the regional total); by 2025, rapid rural-to-urban migration and petroleum-financed administrative concentration expanded this northern corridor to 533,9k inhabitants (103,95 persons per km²). The Western Border Districts and Oecusse grew from 224,4k in 1975 to 477,7k in 2025 (78,48 persons per km²), anchored by agrarian coffee highlands in Ermera and border market towns in Bobonaro and Cova Lima. The Eastern Districts (Baucau, Lautem, Viqueque and Manufahi) expanded from 184,8k in 1975 to 393,4k in 2025 (69,09 persons per km²). This study synthesises 780 catalogued settlements with multi-decade national censuses, truth commission conflict records and remote sensing land cover data to establish a rigorous spatial baseline of modern Timorese demographic evolution.

# Background

## Decolonisation Crisis and the Indonesian Invasion (1975-1979)

The modern demographic history of East Timor began amidst the rapid collapse of the Portuguese colonial empire [@Feij2022Autodeterminao]. Following the Lisbon military coup of 25 April 1974, Portuguese colonial administrators initiated a decentralised decolonisation process, permitting the formation of indigenous political associations [@Feij2022Autodeterminao; @Smith2002Timor]. Three principal factions emerged: the Democratic Union of Timor (UDT), advocating initial federation with Lisbon; the Revolutionary Front for Independent East Timor (Fretilin), championing immediate sovereignty and agrarian reform; and the Timorese Popular Democratic Association (Apodeti), supporting integration into Indonesia as an autonomous province. Tensions escalated into armed factional fighting in August 1975, causing several thousand fatalities and the flight of colonial governor Mario Lemos Pires to Atauro Island [@Olsson2009Chapter].

Having established de facto territorial control by September 1975, Fretilin declared the Democratic Republic of Timor-Leste (RDTL) on 28 November 1975 in response to cross-border incursions by Indonesian special forces. On 7 December 1975, the Indonesian military launched Operasi Seroja (Operation Lotus), seizing Dili through simultaneous amphibious landings and paratroop drops [@Schulze2024East]. Civilian populations fled the capital in panic, seeking sanctuary in the rugged mountain interior. Indonesian forces occupied coastal towns including Baucau, Liquiçá and Manatuto before advancing inland along main transit arteries. In July 1976, Jakarta enacted legislation formally annexing the territory as Indonesia's 27th province (Timor Timur), an action rejected by the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council [@Smith2002Timor; @Feij2022Autodeterminao].

Between late 1977 and 1979, the Indonesian armed forces launched Operasi Kikis and Operasi Keamanan, comprehensive encirclement and annihilation campaigns designed to crush guerrilla resistance and isolate mountain civilian populations [@Olsson2009Chapter; @Schulze2024East]. Deployed aircraft subjected interior ridge lines to persistent aerial bombardment, destroying terraced food plots, livestock and water catchments. Deprived of agrarian harvest cycles and forced into progressively marginal upland terrain, hundreds of thousands of displaced villagers faced acute famine. By late 1978, resistance perimeters collapsed on Mount Matebian in Baucau and Mount Kablaki in Same, forcing emaciated survivors down to Indonesian reception checkpoints [@Linton2019Internatio].

## Military Occupation, Resettlement Camps and Demographic Mortality (1979-1989)

Following military encirclement, Indonesian authorities instituted a nationwide policy of forced resettlement (*pemukiman kembali*). Civilians were barred from returning to their ancestral hamlets (*knua*) in isolated highlands and were instead concentrated along patrolled vehicular roads, military posts and arid coastal flats [@Linton2019Internatio; @Robinson2018People]. In these strategic hamlets, movement was restricted by military curfew and travel permits (*surat jalan*), preventing cultivators from clearing fields beyond a narrow security cordon [@Robinson2018People]. 

The demographic consequences of displacement and internment were devastating [@Linton2019Internatio]. In internment camps such as Lautém, Natarbora and Hatolia, overcrowding, contaminated surface water and near-total absence of medical supplies produced explosive epidemics of bacillary dysentery, malaria, tuberculosis and beriberi. Independent investigations by the Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation in East Timor (CAVR) estimated conflict-related excess mortality between 1975 and 1999 at 102.800 to 183.000 deaths, with the overwhelming majority occurring during the acute famine phase of 1977 to 1980 [@Linton2019Internatio; @Robinson2018People].

By 1980, the Indonesian census recorded a provincial population of only 555.000 persons, down from 660.000 in 1975. This documented deficit reflects both direct battle casualties and catastrophic indirect famine mortality. During the 1980s, the administration initiated pacification programmes, investing in asphalt road corridors, primary schools and district health clinics (*puskesmas*) [@Guelke2000South]. While state-sponsored transmigration brought several thousand civil servants and traders from Java, Sulawesi and West Timor, native Timorese fertility rebounded sharply, restoring positive natural increase and lifting regional population to 748k by 1990.

## Resistance Networks, the Santa Cruz Massacre and Diplomatic Internationalisation (1989-1999)

In 1989, Indonesian authorities declared East Timor an open province, lifting special travel restrictions in an attempt to project normalisation to the international community. This opening facilitated visits by foreign dignitaries, including Pope John Paul II in October 1989, which galvanized youth nationalist mobilisations across Dili. Under the strategic leadership of Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão, the armed wing (Falintil) was restructured into a non-partisan national army, while clandestine civilian networks coordinated political demonstrations across urban centres [@Lundry2022East; @Guimares2019Lngua].

On 12 November 1991, Indonesian security forces opened fire on a peaceful memorial procession at the Santa Cruz cemetery in Dili, killing more than 250 unarmed youths. Captured on film by foreign video journalists Max Stahl and Bob Muntz, footage of the massacre was broadcast internationally, puncturing Jakarta's narrative of peaceful integration [@Lundry2022East; @Fernandes2022Australias]. International solidarity movements surged, pressuring Western governments over military export licences. In 1996, the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded jointly to Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo and diplomatic representative José Ramos-Horta, cementing international recognition of the self-determination struggle [@RamosHorta2023Timor].

## The 1999 Popular Consultation, Scorched-Earth Destruction and UNTAET Transition

The Asian financial crisis of 1997 to 1998 and the subsequent resignation of President Suharto in May 1998 altered the political landscape. In January 1999, incoming Indonesian President B. J. Habibie announced that East Timor would be permitted to choose between wide-ranging autonomy within Indonesia or full independence. The United Nations Mission in East Timor (UNAMET) was established under Resolution 1246 to conduct the popular consultation. Despite widespread intimidation and violence orchestrated by military-backed militias (such as Aitarak in Dili and Besi Merah Putih in Liquiçá), 98,6% of registered voters turned out on 30 August 1999, with 78,5% voting decisively to reject the proposed autonomy framework.

Within hours of the announcement on 4 September 1999, Indonesian military units and auxiliary militias initiated Operasi Guntur (Operation Thunder), a coordinated scorched-earth campaign. Over 70% of public buildings, electrical substations, water supply mains, bridges and private houses were systematically burned or dynamited. More than 1.400 civilians were killed in targeted massacres, notably in churches at Suai and Liquiçá. Over 250k residents were forcibly transported at gunpoint across the land border into makeshift camps in West Timor, while hundreds of thousands more fled into mountain forests [@Damaledo2018Divided; @Koefner2000Displaceme].

Confronted with international outrage, the UN Security Council authorised Resolution 1264, deploying the Australian-led International Force East Timor (INTERFET) on 20 September 1999 to restore security. In October 1999, the Indonesian People's Consultative Assembly formally revoked the 1976 annexation decree, and UN Resolution 1272 established UNTAET as an interim sovereign governing authority. Over the ensuing two years, UN agencies, international peacekeepers and humanitarian non-governmental organisations supervised the repatriation of over 200k refugees from West Timor, reconstructed physical infrastructure and prepared the civil service for self-government [@Koefner2000Displaceme; @Vieira2015Timor; @Auweraert2012Introducti].

## Restoration of Sovereignty, Petroleum Revenues and Dili Urban Primacy (2002-2026)

On 20 May 2002, the Democratic Republic of Timor-Leste celebrated the formal restoration of its sovereignty, with Xanana Gusmão sworn in as first constitutional president. The newly independent nation inherited a devastated economy and an impoverished population. However, the ratification of maritime boundary agreements and the development of offshore hydrocarbon deposits in the Timor Sea (notably the Bayu-Undan and Greater Sunrise fields) transformed the national fiscal balance [@Scheiner2022Resource]. In 2005, parliament established the Petroleum Fund of Timor-Leste, an offshore sovereign wealth repository designed to manage petrodollar revenues and finance public capital investment [@Pereira2018Timorleste; @Scheiner2022Resource].

State revenues were directed into road rehabilitation, rural electrification, educational expansion and social protection cash transfers [@Pereira2018Timorleste]. Yet the concentration of administrative institutions, university campuses and commercial activity in Dili stimulated massive internal migration, precipitating rapid urbanisation that outpaced water and sanitation infrastructure [@McWilliam2015Rural; @Carvalho2025Impact]. Political-military fractures resurfaced during the 2006 crisis, when the dismissal of 591 soldiers sparked factional clashes between westerners (*kaladi*) and easterners (*firaku*), displacing 150k civilians into temporary tent camps across Dili until national reconciliation and institutional reform restored political stability [@Auweraert2012Introducti; @Vieira2015Timor].

Between 2004 and 2025, East Timor maintained one of the fastest demographic expansion rates in South-East Asia [@Saikia2011Investigation]. An intense post-war baby boom, coupled with declining infant and under-five mortality, drove national population from 923k in 2004 to 1,4M by 2025 [@Saikia2011Investigation; @McWilliam2015Rural].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Terrestrial Mask

MANDALA partitions the national territory of East Timor into 233 active terrestrial grid cells at 5-arcminute spatial resolution (equivalent to approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km per grid cell). The spatial boundary encompasses 16.917 km² of land area, incorporating:
- The eastern main body of Timor Island (14.874 km²), bounded by the Mota Ain and Mota Babulu river frontiers with Indonesian West Timor.
- The coastal exclave of Oecusse Ambeno (815 km²), completely surrounded on its landward perimeter by Indonesian Nusa Tenggara Timur.
- Atauro Island (140 km²), situated 25 km north of Dili across the deep Ombai Strait.
- Jaco Island (10 km²), situated at the easternmost tip of Lautém within Nino Konis Santana National Park [@Anonymous2022Democratic].

Environmental covariates governing the dasymetric weighting surface include digital elevation models, slope gradients, distance to perennial river channels (such as the Loes, Laclo, Seical and Tafara rivers) and road network accessibility. Rugged montane topography along the central Ramelau Range (peaking at Mount Tatamailau, 2.963 metres above sea level) imposes steep transport costs, constraining settlement densities outside intramontane river basins and coastal terraces [@Carvalho2025Impact]. In comparative regional demographic studies across the wider maritime zone, geostatistical interpolation of historical settlement density builds upon verified regional gazetteers and inventories, including Thailand FADGIS, Indonesia Kemendikbud Cagar Budaya, the Harvard Published Excavations Atlas, the Myanmar Bagan Inventory and NUSARC/Dutch OV archival records.

## Settlement Subtraction and Dasymetric Allocation

To isolate nucleated municipal populations from dispersed rural cultivators, 780 catalogued settlements are georeferenced to exact WGS84 coordinates. For each benchmark year between 1975 and 2025, settlement populations are evaluated against national census returns, administrative post registers and colonial parish gazetteers.

At each benchmark interval, the sum of active settlement populations within each sub-region is deducted from the sub-regional demographic envelope. The remaining rural population is then allocated dasymetrically across non-settled grid cells in accordance with environmental suitability indices. A multi-pass boundary-smoothing kernel prevents unnatural density steps across administrative borders while respecting physical mountain divides.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and benchmark population total incorporates explicit uncertainty bounds calibrated to historical data quality:
- The 1975-1980 wartime interval carries a +/- 3% uncertainty envelope, reflecting documentation variances between Portuguese parish registries, Indonesian military provincial tallies and truth commission excess mortality models.
- The 1990-1999 transition carries +/- 3% bounds, accommodating irregular transmigration flows and displaced household numbers prior to the 1999 referendum.
- The 2004-2025 post-independence sequence carries +/- 3% bounds, calibrated against official national census enumerations in 2004, 2010, 2015 and 2022.

# Testing and Validation

## Census Reconciliations and Conflict Mortality Auditing

Reconstructing the demographic trajectory of East Timor requires harmonising data across three distinct political and administrative regimes: late colonial Portuguese civil records, Indonesian provincial censuses (*Sensus Penduduk Indonesia*) and sovereign post-independence censuses conducted by the Direcção-Geral de Estatística (DGE) [@Linton2019Internatio]. 

The catastrophic population decline between 1975 and 1980 was subject to intense international debate during the occupation period. While early church estimates cited losses exceeding 200k persons, demographic analyses conducted by the CAVR Truth Commission utilised retrospective household surveys, cemetery inventories and gravestone counts to construct mortality hazard curves [@Linton2019Internatio; @Robinson2018People]. Their findings documented 18.600 unlawful killings and disappearances alongside a minimum of 84.200 excess deaths caused by hunger and disease, yielding a central conflict mortality estimate of 102.800 persons [@Robinson2018People]. This figure corresponds closely to the 105.000 net population loss recorded in MANDALA between the 1975 baseline (660k) and the 1980 census benchmark (555k).

Post-independence censuses conducted in 2004, 2010, 2015 and 2022 provide comprehensive demographic control. Analysis of age-sex pyramids confirms a pronounced demographic dent in cohorts born between 1975 and 1980, reflecting both elevated infant mortality and suppressed fertility during the acute famine phase [@Saikia2011Investigation]. This contraction is followed by an expansive youth demographic bulge from 2000 onward, confirming high post-conflict marital fertility rates that exceeded 7 children per woman in 2003 before gradually moderating to 4,2 by 2022 [@Saikia2011Investigation; @H2022Participatory; @Lover2014Demographi].

## Geological, Hydrological and Environmental Constraints

Demographic carrying capacity across East Timor is constrained by rugged orogeny, fragile soils and erratic hydroclimate [@Carvalho2025Impact]. The island of Timor represents an active accretionary prism formed by the ongoing collision between the Australian continental margin and the Banda volcanic arc, producing steep, tectonically active mountain ranges and uplifted limestone terraces. Tropical monsoon rainfall is heavily seasonal: northern coastal areas receive less than 1.000 mm annually with a prolonged six-month dry season, while high central ridges receive upwards of 2.500 mm.

In the Dili metropolitan basin, seasonal flash floods discharge down short, steep river catchments (such as the Comoro and Bitaque rivers), depositing coarse gravel and eroding fragile riparian banks [@Carvalho2025Impact]. Over-extraction of groundwater from shallow alluvial aquifers has induced localised saltwater intrusion along Dili Bay, while land subsidence and coastal mangrove loss heighten urban vulnerability [@Tai2026Twin]. In the capital's eastern suburbs, environmental contamination of urban water bodies such as Lake Joao Paulo II poses direct public health hazards for informal residential settlements [@Branco2025Environmen]. Beyond the capital, secondary urban centres such as Baucau depend on fragile karst springs, where community water management systems mediate access between upland hamlets and urban commercial quarters [@Palmer2010Enlivening]. Across interior districts, steep slopes and thin lithosols exacerbate soil erosion when swidden cultivators clear hillside plots, encouraging agroforestry diversification into cashew and leguminous tree crops to stabilise fragile soils [@L2022Diversity].

## Sociolinguistic and Religious Demography

Sociolinguistic patterns across the territory reflect complex layers of Austronesian and Papuan ethnolinguistic settlement [@Smith2002Timor; @Guimares2019Lngua]. The 2010 and 2015 national censuses document over thirty distinct indigenous language varieties. Tetum Prasa (Dili Tetum), an Austronesian creole developed as an administrative and trade lingua franca during Portuguese rule, serves as the dominant inter-ethnic language and is co-official alongside Portuguese [@Guimares2019Lngua]. While Portuguese was restored as an official language of administration and law, the widespread educational use of Indonesian during the occupation established lasting bilingualism among older cohorts [@Muliana2026Pelatihan]. In eastern districts, Papuan languages such as Fataluku (in Lautém), Makasae (in Baucau and Viqueque) and Makalero predominate, while Mambai occupies the central highlands of Ainaro and Ermera, and Baikenu characterizes the Oecusse exclave.

Religious affiliation underwent a profound transformation during the Indonesian period [@Coutinho2024Alimentao]. In 1975, less than 30% of the population was formally Catholic, with the majority adhering to traditional animist ancestor beliefs (*lulik*) centered around sacred houses (*uma lulik*) and botanical healing traditions [@Almeida2024Symbology; @Coutinho2024Alimentao]. Because Indonesian state ideology (*Pancasila*) required all citizens to register under one of five recognised monotheistic religions, and because the Catholic Church conducted services in Tetum rather than Bahasa Indonesia, hundreds of thousands of Timorese embraced Catholicism as an expression of cultural and national identity. By 2002, over 96% of the population was Catholic, combining Christian liturgy with customary ritual practices, while small Protestant and Muslim minorities remained active in urban centres [@Coutinho2024Alimentao].

## Cross-Border Dynamics and Infrastructure Modernisation

Cross-border mobility between East Timor and Indonesian West Timor (Nusa Tenggara Timur) remains an important economic and social factor [@Damaledo2018Divided]. Families divided by the 1904 and 1916 Portuguese-Dutch border treaties maintain customary ties across the frontier, exchanging agricultural produce, livestock and consumer goods at border posts such as Batugade, Salele and Bobonaro [@Damaledo2018Divided]. Bilateral cooperation on border demarcation, transit corridors to the Oecusse exclave and regional trade integration has steadily deepened, supported by diplomatic partnerships across the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) [@RamosHorta2023Timor]. In Oecusse, the Special Administrative Region of Oecusse Ambeno (RAEOA) has pioneered state investments in international airport infrastructure, coastal roads and community tourism initiatives in Pante Makasar [@Tosun2025Influence; @Tosun2025Multistakeholder].

National reconstruction programmes since 2002 have prioritised road network asphalt paving, bridge construction and digital connectivity [@Pereira2018Timorleste]. State investments in telecommunications, cellular coverage and electrical distribution have integrated peripheral mountain settlements into the national economy, supporting mobile banking, emergency medical evacuation and educational access. Crucially, the establishment of clear land title registries under Law Number 13 of 2017 has provided legal certainty for commercial development and municipal planning in Dili and regional capitals [@Silva2021Legal], stimulating enterprise in agro-industrial processing, specialty coffee export and hospitality [@Silva2023Timorlestes].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger for East Timor was established through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion protocol designed to capture every municipal, administrative post and suco settlement across all thirteen municipalities:
- Wave 1: Ingestion of official national censuses (2004, 2010, 2015, 2022) and administrative registry gazetteers from the Direcção Nacional de Estatística, establishing 484 georeferenced settlement centroids.
- Wave 2: Archival extraction from Portuguese colonial cartography, mission parish registers and Indonesian provincial administrative listings, adding 211 historical settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, adding 85 historical village and administrative post centres.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and homonym audits across all three divisions, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 794 candidate records were evaluated: 780 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 14 were excluded (comprising duplicate homonyms and subordinate suburbs merged within a 2,2 km spatial radius).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic history of East Timor from 1975 to 2026 exhibits three sharply defined structural phases: acute conflict contraction (1975-1980), gradual pacification recovery (1980-1999) and explosive post-independence expansion (1999-2026) (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### Invasion, Encirclement and Acute Famine (1975 to 1980)

The first phase was characterized by military disruption and mortality [@Schulze2024East]. Following the December 1975 invasion, fighting spread across the country, forcing hundreds of thousands of villagers into mountain interiors. Between 1977 and 1979, encirclement campaigns destroyed traditional food production systems, while forced relocation into internment camps produced widespread famine and disease epidemics [@Linton2019Internatio; @Robinson2018People].

Regional population fell from 660k in 1975 to 555k in 1980, an absolute loss of 105.000 persons (-15,9% net decline). All three sub-regions suffered proportional losses: Dili and the Central North Coast contracted from 250,8k to 210,9k (-39,9k); the Western Border Districts and Oecusse fell from 224,4k to 188,7k (-35,7k); and the Eastern Districts declined from 184,8k to 155,4k (-29,4k). The loss of productive adults and widespread child mortality left lasting imbalances in the demographic age structure.

### Military Consolidation and Slow Demographic Recovery (1980 to 1990)

During the 1980s, the Indonesian administration consolidated territorial control. Internment camp inmates were permitted to cultivate land near roadside settlements, and state health programmes gradually curtailed infectious disease outbreaks through basic district health clinics (*puskesmas*) [@Robinson2018People; @N2014Implementing]. Subsidised rice shipments from Java alleviated acute starvation, while expanded school networks and public works generated employment in district towns [@Guelke2000South].

High marital fertility fuelled a demographic rebound. Regional population climbed from 555k in 1980 to 748k in 1990 (+34,8% increase over the decade), surpassing the pre-war population baseline. Dili Metropolitan and the Central North Coast reached 284,2k, Western Border Districts reached 254,3k and the Eastern Districts reached 209,4k. Immigration by Indonesian civil servants, police, military personnel and Bugis-Makassar traders added approximately 30k non-indigenous residents, predominantly concentrated in Dili and Baucau.

### Urban Resurgence, Referendum and Mass Displacement (1990 to 1999)

The decade from 1990 to 1999 witnessed accelerating urban concentration in Dili alongside heightened political mobilisation. Dili's municipal population expanded rapidly as rural youths moved to the capital for secondary and higher education, joining clandestine pro-independence student networks [@Lundry2022East]. Regional population reached 850k by mid-1999 (yielding 50,25 persons per km²).

The August 1999 referendum and subsequent retaliatory violence caused severe demographic dislocation. Over 250k Timorese were forcibly moved into West Timor, while several hundred thousand took refuge in mountain forests [@Damaledo2018Divided; @Koefner2000Displaceme]. An estimated 1.400 civilians were murdered by militias and soldiers. Over 70% of physical structures were destroyed. The demographic shock was temporary: international intervention under INTERFET quickly restored security, and by 2001 over 80% of displaced refugees had returned to their home communities [@Koefner2000Displaceme; @Vieira2015Timor].

### Post-Independence Baby Boom, Petroleum Economy and Dili Primacy (1999 to 2026)

The restoration of full sovereignty in 2002 initiated a period of sustained demographic expansion. National population grew from 923k in 2004 to 1,07M in 2010, 1,18M in 2015, 1,34M in 2022 and 1,4M in 2025. This rapid growth was driven by an extraordinary post-war baby boom, with total fertility rates exceeding 7 children per woman in the early 2000s, reflecting peace, family reunification and early marriage [@Saikia2011Investigation; @Barnes2018Book].

Concurrently, oil revenues from Timor Sea gas fields funded national infrastructure projects and public sector payrolls, drawing tens of thousands of rural migrants into Dili [@Scheiner2022Resource; @McWilliam2015Rural]. By 2025, Dili Metropolitan and the Central North Coast accommodated 533,9k residents (38% of the national total; 103,95 persons per km²). The Western Border Districts reached 477,7k (78,48 persons per km²), and the Eastern Districts grew to 393,4k (69,09 persons per km²) [@McWilliam2015Rural; @Cabasset2025Neuvime].

The settlement hierarchy reflects extreme urban primacy focused on the national capital:
1. National capital metropolis (> 100k inhabitants): Dili urban area, encompassing the administrative posts of Dom Aleixo (130,1k peak), Cristo Rei (62,8k), Vera Cruz (36,5k) and Nain Feto (28,5k), concentrating over 250k residents within the contiguous coastal plain.
2. Major regional and municipal capitals (50k to 125k peak inhabitants): Ermera (125,7k peak), Baucau (123,2k peak), Bobonaro (97,8k peak), Ainaro (74,9k peak), Viqueque (73k peak), Liquiçá (71,9k peak), Oe-Cusse Ambeno (68,9k peak), Lautém (65,2k peak), Manatuto (55,3k peak) and Manufahi (53,7k peak).
3. Secondary administrative post centres (20k to 50k inhabitants): Maliana in Bobonaro (32,4k), Suai in Cova Lima (25,2k), Gleno in Ermera (22,8k), Pante Makassar in Oecusse (37,3k), Lospalos in Lautém (29,2k) and Same in Manufahi (30,5k).
4. Tertiary rural suco centres and agrarian villages (< 20k inhabitants): hundreds of coffee-farming hamlets, coastal fishing villages and highland settlements distributed across the interior.

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis for East Timor remains subject to specific evidentiary constraints:
1. Disrupted archival continuity: the scorched-earth destruction of September 1999 resulted in the widespread burning of municipal archives, land registries, parish books and census records, necessitating heavy reliance on central Indonesian census publications, property tenure reconstructions and post-conflict retrospective surveys [@Silva2021Legal].
2. Boundary changes and administrative restructuring: Portuguese concelhos and postos were reorganised under Indonesian rule into kabupatens and kecamatans, and subsequently reconfigured post-2002 into municipalities (*municípios*) and administrative posts (*postos administrativos*), complicating longitudinal tract-level comparisons.
3. Unregistered vital events during wartime: births, infant deaths and displacement mortality between 1975 and 1980 went largely unrecorded by formal state registries, requiring demographic reconstruction models to derive conflict mortality from cohort-survival projections.
4. Internal displacement and dual residency: circular labour migration between rural sucos and informal Dili settlements creates seasonal variations in municipal census counts [@McWilliam2015Rural].

# Conclusion

East Timor experienced a dramatic demographic transition across the half-century spanning 1975 to 2026. The catastrophic population collapse from 660k in 1975 to 555k in 1980 stands as one of the sharpest conflict-induced demographic contractions in post-war Asian history, caused by aerial bombardment, forced displacement and severe famine during Indonesian military encirclement. Following pacification in the 1980s, the population rebounded to 748k in 1990 and 850k in 1999.

Despite the destruction of 70% of national infrastructure and the forced deportation of a quarter-million civilians following the 1999 independence referendum, sovereign statehood in 2002 initiated a period of sustained demographic expansion. Driven by a post-war baby boom, total fertility rates exceeded 7 children per woman in the early 2000s, carrying national population to 1,4M by 2025 across 16.917 km² of territory. By integrating 780 catalogued settlements with multi-decade national censuses and conflict mortality records, MANDALA establishes a systematic demographic baseline for Timor-Leste's historical geography and state-building.
